title: Calculus II: Series and Differential Equations
description: New functions and techniques, infinite series from geometric sums to Taylor polynomials, and differential equations from cooling coffee to oscillators.
audience: A capable adult who has met limits, derivatives of powers, the chain rule, antiderivatives and areas in Discere's calculus course. Exponentials, logarithms, sines, the product rule, substitution and parts are covered here, since the first course stops before them.
outcomes: You'll be able to differentiate and integrate exponentials, logarithms, sines and cosines, using the product rule, substitution and parts.
You'll be able to sum a geometric series and choose a test to decide whether a series converges.
You'll be able to bound the error of an alternating series and of a Taylor polynomial.
You'll be able to find a power series's radius of convergence and use series to evaluate an integral.
You'll be able to solve exponential, separable and logistic equations, step any first-order equation with Euler's method and solve a linear oscillator.

NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, Chapter 4 Elementary Functions
Verhulst, Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement (1838)

modules.title: More functions to work with
modules.summary: Exponentials, products, substitution, parts and waves: the functions and techniques series and differential equations need.

modules.title: Infinite sums
modules.summary: When adding forever settles, how to test it, and how functions become power series.

modules.title: Differential equations
modules.summary: Rates that depend on the state: models, exact solutions, stepping by hand and in code, and oscillators.

lessons.title: Growth that feeds itself
lessons.objective: Differentiate exponentials and logarithms and say why e is special.

concepts.title: Derivative of e^x
concepts.summary: d/dx e^x = e^x; with the chain rule, d/dx e^(kx) = k e^(kx).

concepts.title: Natural logarithm
concepts.summary: ln x undoes e^x and d/dx ln x = 1/x; d/dx a^x = a^x ln a.

misconceptions: The derivative of e^x is x e^(x-1). The power rule does not apply when x is the exponent.
e is just another number. It is the base whose own slope at 0 is exactly 1.
ln x is a different quantity from log base 10. It is the log to base e; the 10 and e logs differ by a constant factor.
sequence: Compound growth: (1 + 1/n)^n for n = 1, 12, 365, ... approaches e = 2.71828.
Slope of a^x at 0 for several a; find the one with slope 1.
State d/dx e^x = e^x and see k from the chain rule.
Inverse: ln x and its derivative 1/x.
Use them to differentiate a^x.
examples: (1 + 1/12)^12 = 2.613; with daily compounding about 2.7146.
d/dx e^(2x) at x = 1 is 2 e^2 = 14.78; d/dx 2^x at x = 0 is ln 2 = 0.693.

figures.shows: tangent on the polynomial approximations of e^x as a degree-4 coefficient list [1,1,0.5,0.1667,0.0417] at x = 0 and x = 1, as a hint of 'slope equals value' near 0.
figures.learnerAction: Switch cases and read slope against height.

figures.shows: Slope of a^x at 0 plotted against a for a from 1.5 to 4.
figures.learnerAction: Hover to find where the slope is 1.

historyNotes: Jacob Bernoulli studied compound interest around 1683 and found the limit that Euler later named e. Euler introduced the letter e in a manuscript of about 1727 to 1728.

lessons.title: Products and substitution
lessons.objective: Differentiate a product and integrate by substitution.

concepts.title: Product rule
concepts.summary: (u v)' = u' v + u v'.

concepts.title: Substitution
concepts.summary: Replace an inner function with u and its derivative with du: the chain rule run backwards.

misconceptions: (u v)' = u' v'. Try u = v = x: (x^2)' = 2x, not 1.
Substitution changes only the integrand. A definite integral's limits must change too, or the answer must be put back in x.
Any integrand can be substituted. It works when the derivative of the inner part is also present.
sequence: Area of a rectangle with changing sides: the two-strip picture for the product rule.
Check the rule on x^2 = x times x.
Substitution as undoing the chain rule: spot an inner function with its derivative beside it.
Change limits in a definite integral.
Know when it fails.
examples: (x e^x)' = e^x + x e^x = (1 + x) e^x; at x = 1 this is 2e = 5.437.
Integral from 0 to 1 of 2x e^(x^2) dx: u = x^2, du = 2x dx, limits 0 to 1, so e^1 - e^0 = e - 1 = 1.718. Integral from 0 to 2 of x/(x^2 + 1) dx = 1/2 ln 5 = 0.805.

figures.shows: area for the polynomial 2x over 0 to 1 and over 0 to 2 as stand-ins for the du part.
A rectangle u by v with strips of width du and dv showing the product rule terms.

questionPlan.sample: What is the derivative of x e^x at x = 1, to two decimals?
What is the integral of 2x e^(x^2) from 0 to 1, to three decimals?
What is the integral of x/(x^2 + 1) from 0 to 2, to three decimals?

lessons.title: Calculus of sine and cosine
lessons.objective: Differentiate and integrate sine and cosine in radians and use the small-angle limit.

concepts.title: Derivative of sine
concepts.summary: d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = -sin x, when x is in radians.

concepts.title: Small-angle limit
concepts.summary: sin x / x tends to 1 as x tends to 0, so sin x is about x for small x in radians.

misconceptions: The derivative formulas hold in any angle unit. In degrees an extra pi/180 appears.
sin 2x has derivative cos 2x. The chain rule adds a factor 2.
The area under sin x from 0 to pi is zero because it is symmetric. The area is 2; the integral is positive on that half-wave.
sequence: Radian recap: 2 pi in a full turn, and x is arc length on the unit circle.
Slope of sine at 0 from the sine graph: 1, which is why sin x is about x.
d/dx sin x = cos x from the graph of the slope.
Chain rule and integrals of cos(kx).
Application: velocity and acceleration of a swinging oscillator.
examples: d/dx sin 3x at x = 0 is 3 cos 0 = 3. Integral from 0 to pi of sin x dx = 2.
Integral from 0 to pi/4 of cos 2x dx = 1/2 sin(pi/2) = 0.5.

figures.shows: sin x and its slope curve cos x, with the slope read off at a draggable point.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the point and compare height of cosine to slope of sine.

figures.shows: limit with polynomial approximations x - x^3/6 over x, hole at 0, as a stand-in for sin x / x.

questionPlan.sample: What is the slope of y = sin 3x at x = 0?
What is the integral of sin x from 0 to pi?
What is the integral of cos 2x from 0 to pi/4?

lessons.title: Integrating a product
lessons.objective: Use integration by parts to integrate a product of a polynomial and an exponential or sine.

concepts.title: Integration by parts
concepts.summary: The integral of u dv equals u v minus the integral of v du: the product rule run backwards.

concepts.title: Choosing u
concepts.summary: Choose u to be the factor that gets simpler when differentiated (a polynomial) and dv the factor you can integrate.

misconceptions: Parts always applies and always simplifies. The wrong choice makes the new integral harder; the polynomial usually goes in u.
The integral of a product is the product of the integrals. It is not; the product rule shows that.
The boundary term v u can be dropped. It carries part of the answer and must be evaluated at the limits.
sequence: Integrate the product rule: (u v)' = u' v + u v'.
Rearrange to the parts formula.
Try x e^x two ways, with u = x and u = e^x.
Definite integrals and the boundary term.
Repeat once for x^2 e^x, noting a pattern.
examples: Integral of x e^x: u = x, dv = e^x dx gives x e^x - e^x = (x - 1) e^x. From 0 to 1: 0 - (-1) = 1.
Integral from 0 to pi of x sin x dx: u = x, v = -cos x gives [-x cos x] + integral of cos x = pi + 0 = pi = 3.142.

figures.shows: Two columns for u and dv with the result of each choice for x e^x.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in the product choices and compare.

questionPlan.sample: What is the integral of x e^x from 0 to 1?

lessons.title: Adding forever
lessons.objective: Sum a geometric series and say when an infinite sum has a finite value.

concepts.title: Partial sums
concepts.summary: The sum of the first n terms; the series converges when these tend to a limit.

concepts.title: Geometric series
concepts.summary: a + ar + ar^2 + ... = a / (1 - r) when |r| < 1, and diverges otherwise.

misconceptions: Adding infinitely many numbers always gives infinity. If the terms shrink fast enough the total is finite.
0.999... is a bit below 1. It is a geometric series with sum 0.9/(1 - 0.1) = 1.
If the terms go to zero, the series converges. This is necessary only; the harmonic series has terms to zero and diverges.
sequence: Zeno's race: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... fills a square of side 1.
Partial sums approach 2 - 1/2^n; the limit is the sum.
General geometric formula via multiply-and-subtract.
When r is 1 or more the partial sums grow.
A bouncing ball: total distance travelled.
examples: A ball dropped from 10 m rebounds to 60 percent of its previous height each time: total distance = 10 + 2 x (6 + 3.6 + 2.16 + ...) = 10 + 2 x 6/0.4 = 40 m.

figures.shows: Partial sums of 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... against n, approaching a dashed line at 2.
Unit square repeatedly halved: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 regions shaded.

questionPlan.sample: What is the sum of 6 + 3.6 + 2.16 + ... where each term is 0.6 times the last?

For which ratio does 1 + r + r^2 + ... converge?

lessons.title: Does it settle?
lessons.objective: Choose and apply a convergence test: divergence, p-series, comparison and ratio.

concepts.title: p-series
concepts.summary: The sum of 1/n^p converges for p > 1 and diverges for p <= 1; the harmonic series (p = 1) diverges.

concepts.title: Ratio test
concepts.summary: If |a(n+1)/a(n)| tends to L, the series converges when L < 1 and diverges when L > 1.

misconceptions: Terms going to zero guarantee convergence. The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... diverges, slowly: it first exceeds 3 after 11 terms.
The ratio test settles everything. At L = 1 it says nothing.
If a series converges, its sum is 'about' where partial sums look like they stop. Slow divergence can hide for thousands of terms.
sequence: Test the harmonic series numerically: sums for n = 10, 100, 1000 climb like ln n.
Group terms to show it diverges.
Compare 1/n^2 with telescoping 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n - 1/(n+1), sum 1.
Ratio test for factorials and powers.
A decision flow: terms to zero? p-series? compare? ratio?
examples: 1/(1 x 2) + 1/(2 x 3) + ... = 1. Sum of n/2^n from 1 to infinity = 2.
For 3^n / n!, the ratio is 3/(n + 1), tending to 0, so it converges. Harmonic partial sum H_11 = 3.02 first exceeds 3.

figures.shows: Partial sums of 1/n and 1/n^2 on the same axes, up to n = 1,000.
Decision order for convergence tests.
figures.learnerAction: Put the tests in a sensible order.

questionPlan.sample: How many terms of 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... are needed before the partial sum first exceeds 3?

lessons.title: Alternating sums and how wrong you are
lessons.objective: Bound the error of an alternating series and decide how many terms are needed.

concepts.title: Alternating series test
concepts.summary: If terms alternate in sign, decrease in size and tend to zero, the series converges.

concepts.title: Error bound
concepts.summary: The error after n terms is at most the size of the first omitted term.

misconceptions: A converging series can be summed exactly by adding terms. Most cannot; you stop and bound the error.
Reordering the terms leaves the sum unchanged. For a conditionally convergent series like 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ..., rearranging can change the sum.
Decreasing terms alone guarantee convergence. They must also alternate and go to zero.
sequence: The alternating harmonic series 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ... bounces round its limit ln 2 = 0.6931.
The partial sums trap the answer between consecutive sums.
Error bound from the next term.
Plan: how many terms for a target error.
Contrast absolute and conditional convergence.
examples: After 4 terms: 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 = 0.5833; the error is at most 1/5 = 0.2, so the sum lies between 0.5833 and 0.7833.
Error less than 0.05 needs 1/(N + 1) < 0.05, so N + 1 > 20 and N = 20 terms.

figures.shows: Alternating partial sums zig-zagging toward ln 2 with the error band.

questionPlan.sample: Using the alternating series 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ..., what is the largest possible error after 4 terms?
How many terms of 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ... guarantee an error less than 0.05?
Which series meets the alternating series test?

lessons.title: Power series
lessons.objective: Find the radius and interval of convergence of a power series.

concepts.title: Power series
concepts.summary: A sum of c(n) (x - a)^n: a polynomial that never stops, whose behaviour depends on x.

concepts.title: Radius of convergence
concepts.summary: The R for which the series converges when |x - a| < R and diverges when |x - a| > R; the ratio test finds it.

misconceptions: The series converges for every x. A power series usually has a finite radius; 1/(1 - x) = 1 + x + x^2 + ... only for |x| < 1.
The endpoints always behave like the interior. They need a separate check.
A power series equals its function where it converges. Outside the radius it diverges even if the function is perfectly defined.
sequence: Start with the geometric series as a function of x.
Where it matches 1/(1 - x), and where it blows up.
Ratio test with x in it gives the radius.
Test the endpoints separately.
Differentiate and integrate term by term.
examples: The sum of x^n / 4^n converges for |x| < 4, so R = 4.
The sum of (x - 1)^n / 2^n converges for |x - 1| < 2; the interval (-1, 3) with right endpoint 3.

figures.shows: Partial sums of 1 + x + x^2 + ... against 1/(1 - x) for degrees 2, 4, 8.

questionPlan.sample: What is the radius of convergence of the sum of x^n / 4^n?

lessons.title: Functions as polynomials
lessons.objective: Build Taylor polynomials and bound their error.

concepts.title: Taylor series
concepts.summary: f(x) = sum of [f^(n)(a) / n!] times (x - a)^n; at a = 0, e^x = sum of x^n / n!.

concepts.title: Error bound
concepts.summary: If |f^(n+1)| <= M on the interval, the error of the degree-n polynomial is at most M |x|^(n+1) / (n+1)!.

misconceptions: More terms always fit better. A fixed polynomial fits near the centre and drifts away; the series has finite radius for some functions.
The coefficient of x^n is the nth derivative. It is the nth derivative divided by n!.
A Taylor series always equals its function. It converges to the function only where the error goes to zero.
sequence: Match a polynomial to a function's value, slope and curvature at one point.
Extract coefficients: f^(n)(0)/n!.
Build e^x, sin x, cos x and ln(1 + x).
Evaluate and compare to a calculator.
Bound the error.
examples: e^x about 0: 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 + ...; at x = 1 with degree 4: 2.7083 (true 2.7183).

figures.shows: primitive/tangent cases built from the e^x coefficients [1,1,0.5,0.1667,0.0417] for degrees 1 to 4 as overlays.
sin x with Taylor polynomials of degree 1, 3, 5.

questionPlan.sample: The Taylor series of e^(2x) about 0 begins 1 + 2x + c x^2 + ... What is c?

historyNotes: Brook Taylor published his general series in Methodus incrementorum in 1715. Colin Maclaurin's name is attached to the series about 0, from his 1742 Treatise of Fluxions.

lessons.title: Putting series to work
lessons.objective: Use series to evaluate an integral with no closed form and to justify an approximation.

concepts.title: Integrate term by term
concepts.summary: A power series can be integrated inside its radius, giving series for integrals with no elementary antiderivative.

concepts.title: Approximation by truncation
concepts.summary: Keep the leading terms where later ones are negligible: sin x ≈ x, 1/(1 + x) ≈ 1 - x.

misconceptions: Integrals with no formula cannot be found. They can be found as accurately as needed with series.
Truncated approximations are rough guesses. The error bound makes them quantified.
Small-angle approximations hold at any angle. sin x = x is within 1 percent only for angles up to about 0.24 rad (14 degrees).
sequence: The Gaussian integral of e^(-x^2) from 0 to 1 has no closed form.
Substitute -x^2 into the e^x series and integrate term by term.
Add terms until the alternating bound is small.
Small-angle pendulum: replace sin theta by theta, and see the error.
Relativistic kinetic energy to 1/2 m v^2 as the first term.
examples: Integral from 0 to 1 of e^(-x^2) dx = 1 - 1/3 + 1/10 - 1/42 + 1/216 - ... = 0.7475 after five terms (true 0.7468).
sin x versus x at 0.24 rad: 0.2377 against 0.2400, a 1 percent difference.

figures.shows: Partial sums of the series for the integral against the true value.
Percentage error of sin x ≈ x against angle in degrees.

lessons.title: Rates that depend on the state
lessons.objective: Model growth, decay and cooling with dy/dt = k y and solve them.

concepts.title: Differential equation
concepts.summary: An equation relating a function to its derivatives; a solution is a function that satisfies it.

concepts.title: Exponential model
concepts.summary: dy/dt = k y has solutions y = y0 e^(kt): doubling time ln 2 / k when k > 0, half-life ln 2 / |k| when k < 0.

misconceptions: The solution is a number. It is a function of time, and a family: one for each starting value.
Doubling time depends on the starting amount. For exponential growth it is the same at any size.
Cooling is linear in time. Newton's law makes the gap shrink exponentially.
sequence: A rate that depends on the amount: bacteria, money, radioactive atoms.
Read a slope field: at each point, the slope.
Guess and verify y = y0 e^(kt).
Doubling time and half-life, link to the radioactive-dating idea.
Newton's law of cooling: T = T_room + (T0 - T_room) e^(-kt).
examples: k = 0.03 per year: doubling time ln 2 / 0.03 = 23.1 years.
Coffee at 90 degrees C in a 20 degrees C room with k = 0.1 per minute: after 10 minutes T = 20 + 70 e^(-1) = 45.75 degrees C.

figures.shows: Slope field for dy/dt = y with three solution curves.
Cooling curve for coffee with the room-temperature asymptote.

questionPlan.sample: A quantity grows at 3 percent per year (dy/dt = 0.03 y). What is its doubling time in years, to one decimal?

lessons.title: Separating variables
lessons.objective: Solve separable equations with an initial condition.

concepts.title: Separable equation
concepts.summary: dy/dx = f(x) g(y) can be rewritten as dy/g(y) = f(x) dx and integrated on both sides.

concepts.title: Initial condition
concepts.summary: A value y(x0) = y0 fixes the constant in the general solution.

misconceptions: Dividing by y is always safe. It loses the solution y = 0 when y can be zero.
Integrating both sides gives two constants. One combined constant is enough.
The constant C is added at the end. It must be fixed before the final step to avoid mistakes after taking exponentials.
sequence: Spot the equations where x terms and y terms can be moved to separate sides.
Integrate each side with its own variable.
Solve for y and fix the constant with the initial condition.
Check by differentiating.
Equilibrium solutions that division hides.

figures.shows: Solution curves y^2 = x^2 + C for several C with the initial condition marked.

questionPlan.sample: dy/dt = -2y with y(0) = 5. What is y(1), to three decimals?

lessons.title: Stepping along a slope
lessons.objective: Approximate a solution with Euler's method by hand and in code.

concepts.title: Euler's method
concepts.summary: Starting at (x0, y0), take steps y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)).

concepts.title: Step size and error
concepts.summary: Smaller steps follow the true curve more closely; Euler's error shrinks roughly in proportion to h.

misconceptions: Euler's method is exact for curves. It follows tangents, so a curving solution drifts away.
A smaller step always gives an exact answer. It reduces the error but never removes it.
Using the slope at the end of the step. Euler uses the slope at the start of the step.
sequence: Follow the slope field with straight segments.
Write the update rule and take one step by hand.
Take five steps and compare with the exact solution of y' = x + y, y(0) = 1.
Halve the step and see the error roughly halve.
Put the rule in a loop in Python.
examples: y' = -y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.5, four steps to x = 2: 0.0625 against exact e^(-2) = 0.1353.

figures.shows: Short Euler loop for y' = -y with an adjustable step size as given cases.
figures.learnerAction: Run with h = 0.5 and h = 0.1 and compare with e^(-2).

figures.shows: Euler path overlaid on the slope field and the exact solution.

questionPlan.sample: y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1. What is y after two steps (at x = 0.2)?

choices: Using the slope at the end of the step

lessons.title: Growth with a limit
lessons.objective: Analyse the logistic equation with equilibria, the steepest growth point and its solution.

concepts.title: Logistic equation
concepts.summary: dP/dt = r P (1 - P / K): growth that slows as P approaches the carrying capacity K.

concepts.title: Equilibria
concepts.summary: Constant solutions where dP/dt = 0: P = 0 (unstable) and P = K (stable).

misconceptions: Populations grow until they hit K and then stop abruptly. Growth slows smoothly and approaches K.
Fastest growth happens at the largest population. It happens at P = K/2, with rate rK/4.
Two equilibria are equally important. P = K attracts nearby solutions; P = 0 repels them.
sequence: Start from exponential growth and add a brake.
Find equilibria and test stability from the sign of dP/dt on each side.
Maximum growth rate at K/2.
Write the closed-form solution (separate with partial fractions, stated).
Fit: use data to find r and K (link to the earlier ecosystems idea).
examples: r = 0.5, K = 1000: maximum growth rate = 0.5 x 1000/4 = 125 per unit time, at P = 500.

figures.shows: S-shaped logistic curves for several P0 with the carrying capacity line, and the phase line P against dP/dt.

questionPlan.sample: r = 0.5 and K = 1,000. What is the largest value of dP/dt, in people per unit time?

For dP/dt = r P (1 - P / K) with r > 0, the equilibrium P = K is
questionPlan.answer: Stable: nearby populations move toward it
choices: Stable: nearby populations move toward it

historyNotes: Pierre-Francois Verhulst introduced the logistic equation in 1838 to model population growth with a limit.

lessons.title: Oscillators
lessons.objective: Solve y'' + w^2 y = 0 and y'' + a y' + b y = 0 by their characteristic equations.

concepts.title: Second-order linear equation
concepts.summary: A constant-coefficient equation y'' + a y' + b y = 0 has solutions e^(r t) where r solves r^2 + a r + b = 0.

concepts.title: Oscillation
concepts.summary: Complex roots give oscillation; for y'' + w^2 y = 0 the solutions are cos(w t) and sin(w t) with period 2 pi / w.

misconceptions: The solution to a second-order equation is one function. It needs two constants, fixed by y(0) and y'(0).
Damping stops oscillation. Light damping still oscillates, with shrinking amplitude; only strong damping does not.
The period depends on how big the swing is. For y'' + w^2 y = 0 it depends only on w.
sequence: A mass on a spring: m y'' = -k y.
Guess y = e^(rt) and get the characteristic equation.
Real roots: exponentials. Imaginary roots: cosine and sine.
Use initial conditions to fix the constants.
Add damping and see the three cases.
examples: 0.5 kg on a spring with k = 200 N/m: y'' + 400 y = 0, w = 20 rad/s, period 2 pi / 20 = 0.314 s. With y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0 the solution is cos 20t.

figures.shows: Solutions for undamped, lightly damped and heavily damped cases with the same start.
motion with acceleration 0 and an initial speed as a baseline for comparison with oscillation.

courseCheck: Mixed items: a derivative or integral that needs the product rule, substitution or parts; a geometric sum; a convergence-test choice; an alternating error bound; a radius of convergence; a Taylor estimate with its bound; a separable initial-value problem; an Euler step or a short Python loop; a logistic maximum; and a characteristic equation. Include two modelling questions (cooling and a population with a limit).
platformNeeds: A series explorer: partial sums against n for a chosen series with the limit and error band drawn. Fallback: graph_plot with fixed cases.

A Taylor explorer: a function overlaid with its Taylor polynomials of selectable degree. calculus_explorer takes only polynomials of degree four or less, so it cannot draw e^x or sin x. Fallback: graph_plot series with the polynomials precomputed.
A slope-field and Euler-path figure: a direction field for dy/dx = f(x, y), a draggable start, step size and the exact solution as overlay. Fallback: graph_plot with fixed cases.
A calculus_explorer extension for exp, ln, sin and cos (a function kind rather than only a polynomial).
